chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi and Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from al-Kinani, and Fadalah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said:

“If a man confesses against himself that he stole, then afterward denies it, cut off his hand, even if he is unwilling. And if he confesses against himself to khamr or false accusation, then afterward denies it, then I would flog him.”
I said: “What do you think—if he confesses against himself to a hadd offense for which rajm is applicable, then afterward denies it, would you stone him?”
He said: “No, but I would have struck him.”

key_terms.أَقَرَّ: confessed or acknowledged against oneself before authority
key_terms.بِخَمْرٍ: regarding khamr, meaning an intoxicant offense
key_terms.جَحَدَ: retracted or denied after having confessed
key_terms.ضَارِبَهُ: one who would strike him, i.e. administer flogging
key_terms.فَٱقْطَعْهُ: apply the legal punishment of amputation for theft
key_terms.فِرْيَةٍ: false accusation or slander subject to hadd
key_terms.ٱلرَّجْمَ: stoning as a legal punishment in the specified case

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if someone confesses to a hadd offense and then retracts the confession?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses legal rulings regarding a person's confession to certain hadd offenses and the effect of later retraction. It distinguishes between theft, khamr, false accusation, and an offense entailing rajm, indicating differing judicial consequences after denial. The report is significant in fiqh for evidentiary rules and the implementation of prescribed punishments.
